---
title: "Comparing ME inequalities across models"
subtitle: "Examples 4.3.b and 4.3.a of Mize and Han (2025): nested models, and separate samples"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

The ME inequality of Mize and Han (2025) summarizes the effect of a nominal
predictor in one number: the average absolute difference in the outcome
across its categories. The `meinequality` option of `mecompare` adds that
summary to the table, and with two models in `models()` the summary is
calculated for each model and the **Difference** row tests whether the
inequality changed. The two most common uses are shown here: nested models
(how much of an inequality is accounted for by mediators) and models fit to
separate samples (has an inequality changed over time). Both examples also
appear on the [`meinequality`](../../meinequality/index.html) site, where the
same tests are run with the `meinequality` command.

## Nested models: how much of a racial-ethnic inequality is accounted for by SES?

How much of the racial-ethnic inequality in functional limitations is
accounted for by education, wealth, and income? Fit the model with and
without those variables, store both, and name them in `models()`. The models
are combined with [`suest2`](../../suest2/index.html) so that the test of the
difference accounts for the two models being estimated on the same data. The
outcome is a count of limitations in instrumental activities of daily living
from the Health and Retirement Study.

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_hrs", clear
drop if missing(iadl, race4cat, collegeB, wealth_w, income_w)

quietly nbreg iadl i.race4cat, vce(robust)
estimates store basemod

quietly nbreg iadl i.race4cat i.collegeB c.wealth_w c.income_w, vce(robust)
estimates store medmod
<</dd_do>>
```

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare i.race4cat, models(basemod medmod) meinequality
<</dd_do>>
```

The first block of the table is the ME inequality in each model and its
**Difference**: the reduction in racial-ethnic inequality once education,
wealth, and income are in the model, with a standard error and p-value. The
blocks beneath it are the contrasts with the base category that the ME
inequality summarizes, each with its own cross-model difference. Because
every row is numbered, [`metest`](../../metest/index.html) can express the
reduction as a proportion of the baseline inequality, with a standard error:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
metest (1 - 2) / 1
<</dd_do>>
```

The same difference is what `meinequality race4cat, models(basemod medmod)`
reports; `mecompare` adds the underlying contrasts and the row numbers for
`metest`.

## Separate samples: has the effect of religion changed over time?

When the two models are fit to different samples -- different groups, or
different time periods -- add the `groups` option. Here the question is
whether religious-tradition differences in willingness to let a gay man speak
in public were larger before 1980 than after 2010. Two logits are fit, one
per period, and `groupnames()` labels the rows.

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear
drop if missing(spkhomo, reltrad, age, woman)

quietly logit spkhomo i.reltrad c.age i.woman if year < 1980, vce(robust)
estimates store premod

quietly logit spkhomo i.reltrad c.age i.woman if year >= 2010, vce(robust)
estimates store postmod
<</dd_do>>
```

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare i.reltrad, models(premod postmod) groups groupnames(Pre1980 Post2010) ///
          meinequality(unweighted)
<</dd_do>>
```

`groups` tells `mecompare` that each model's estimation sample is a
different group, so each ME inequality is averaged over that period's own
respondents, and the **Difference** row tests whether the inequality
changed. It is significantly smaller after 2010 than before 1980: religious
traditions have converged on this question.

`unweighted` is used so that the comparison reflects the marginal effects
alone. The default ME inequality weights each pairwise contrast by the share
of the sample in the two categories being contrasted; with `groups`, each
model uses the shares in *its own* sample, so the weighted difference would
also pick up the change in the religious makeup of the GSS between the two
periods. `meinequality(all)` reports both statistics.

## Reference

> Mize, Trenton D. and Bing Han. 2025. "Inequality and Total Effect Summary
> Measures for Nominal and Ordinal Variables." *Sociological Science* 12:
> 115--157.
